solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Words of old chief end when son interrupts (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The clue's plural names the practice of using old words; ARCHAISM covers both one old word and that habit.

indicatorNotes.interrupts: To interrupt is to break in on something, so S breaks into the middle of AIM.

blocks.note: arch = chief, as in archenemy
an end is an aim or goal; S goes in after AI
s = son, the genealogical abbreviation

annotation.surface: An old tribal chief's final words cut short by his son.
annotation.walkthrough: "Words of old chief" reads as one phrase about a chief's last speech, but "Words of old" is the whole definition and "chief" starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: An archaism is a word or phrase from an older stage of the language, still used for effect.

indicatorNotes.following: In a down clue, what follows comes after, so MO sits below AM.

blocks.note: a.m. = morning
a mo = a moment, a little time

annotation.surface: A quick break just after the morning rounds, as a doctor or postman might take.
annotation.walkthrough: "Rounds" looks like a doctor's ward rounds after "morning"; here it means bullets.
annotation.definitionFit: Ammo is short for ammunition, and rounds are units of it.

indicatorNotes.around: Here "around" means turned round, so RAN is read backwards as NAR.
indicatorNotes.wearing: Whoever wears something has it on the outside, so CADS go round NAR.

blocks.note: a heel is a cad, a man who behaves badly
rushed = ran; turned round, NAR goes inside CA...DS

annotation.surface: Con men in a hurry, dressed in high heels.
annotation.walkthrough: "Heels" suggests shoes, but it means rotters, cads. "Frauds" is the definition in the sense of hoaxes, not people.
annotation.definitionFit: A canard is a false story put about to deceive, which is a kind of fraud.

blocks.note: of Attica, the region round Athens, whose dialect was classical Greek
the top flight of stairs ends in the room under the roof

annotation.surface: A Greek airline passenger's last journey home.
annotation.walkthrough: "Flight" suggests an aeroplane; the question mark warns that it is a flight of stairs.
annotation.definitionFit: The attic is the room under the roof, where the top flight of stairs ends.

indicatorNotes.Broadcast: To broadcast seed is to scatter it, so the letters are scattered and re-sown.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

annotation.surface: A description of how programmes are sent out to our screens.
annotation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the whole clue describes the answer, and the same words also scatter "serving to media" into it.
annotation.definitionFit: Streaming video is broadcast content served over the internet to devices and media players.

blocks.note: Shakespeare's braggart ensign in Henry IV Part 2 and Henry V; 'ancient' was his rank
the firearm duellists faced each other with at dawn

annotation.surface: An old weapon Shakespeare might have described in a duel scene.
annotation.walkthrough: "Ancient" looks like an adjective meaning old; in Shakespeare it is a rank, an ensign, and Pistol holds it.
annotation.definitionFit: Pistol is Falstaff's swaggering ensign, called Ancient Pistol; a pistol is also a handgun used in duels.

entries.clue: Likely to get business, almost squeal about it (2,4,3)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost stops just short, so INFORM loses its last letter.
indicatorNotes.about: About means surrounding, so INFOR goes round LINE.

blocks.note: squeal = inform (to the police); almost drops the M
one's line is one's business, as in 'what line are you in?'

annotation.surface: Someone about to land a deal who can hardly keep from shouting about it.
annotation.walkthrough: "it" stands for "business": the word order is definition, then "business", then the squeal that goes round it.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to be next in the queue for a prize or post is to be likely to get it.

entries.clue: Under property, men will find snake in the grass (7)

indicatorNotes.Under: In a down clue, what is under comes lower, so OR follows TRAIT.

blocks.note: a property is a characteristic, a trait
OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

annotation.surface: Workmen digging under a house who turn up a snake in the grass.
annotation.walkthrough: "Property" suggests land or a house, but it means a quality.
annotation.definitionFit: A snake in the grass is a treacherous person hiding behind friendliness: a traitor.

blocks.note: to last is to go on, continue
to ditch is to abandon

annotation.surface: Advice to keep going but give up the final, as a team might be told.
annotation.walkthrough: "final" looks like a noun, the match; it is the adjective, as in a last-ditch effort.
annotation.definitionFit: A last-ditch attempt is the final one, made when all else has failed.

blocks.note: to contract an illness is to get it
a ship's captain commands from the bridge

annotation.surface: A team captain being told which position to play in a match.
annotation.walkthrough: "Captain" and "game" suggest a sports team; the captain is at sea.
annotation.definitionFit: Contract bridge is the standard form of the card game bridge.

blocks.note: to watch = to keep under observation
a display = a computer screen

annotation.walkthrough: "Watch display" reads like the face of a wristwatch; split it into a verb and a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: Monitor means to keep watch on, and a monitor is the screen that displays a computer's output.

entries.clue: River bank in huge French city (7)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts R LEAN inside O...S.

blocks.note: OS = outsize, the clothing label for very large
r = river, as on maps
an aircraft banks when it leans over in a turn

annotation.surface: A river bank in a big French city, like the quays along the Seine.
annotation.walkthrough: "River bank" reads as one thing; "bank" is a verb here, to tilt.
annotation.definitionFit: Orléans is a city on the Loire in central France.

entries.clue: Delayed parts I don’t care about (14)

indicatorNotes.about: About can mean around and all over the place, so the letters are moved around.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

annotation.surface: Someone putting off the bits of a job they can't be bothered with.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface shows the answer in action: shirking the parts you don't care about is how you end up procrastinating.
annotation.definitionFit: To procrastinate is to delay doing something you ought to do.

entries.clue: Lead, with another one, around country (5,4)

blocks.note: a co-star shares the lead role with another actor
I = one, the Roman numeral
ca. = circa, around (a date)

annotation.surface: Two people sharing the lead as they travel around a country.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas suggest "with another one" belongs together; the break falls after "another", and "around" is a piece, not a container.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer is one particular Central American republic.

blocks.note: a vice is a workbench clamp
lowered = down

annotation.surface: A question about what brings the level of crime down.
annotation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: read straight, a crackdown is what reduces vice; read as a recipe, a vice (CLAMP) lowered (DOWN) spells it.
annotation.definitionFit: A clampdown is a firm official crackdown, the kind of thing that gets wrongdoing reduced.

blocks.note: to fear = in an older sense, to anticipate with dread
to capture = to arrest, as police do a suspect

annotation.walkthrough: The fear sense survives mostly in apprehension and apprehensive.
annotation.definitionFit: Apprehend means both to arrest someone and to anticipate something with fear.

entries.clue: Original way to go east of Douglas? (5)

indicatorNotes.east of: In an across clue east is to the right, so ST comes after FIR.

blocks.note: a Douglas is a Douglas fir; the question mark flags the definition by example
St = street, a way

annotation.surface: A route heading east of Douglas, the capital of the Isle of Man.
annotation.walkthrough: Douglas looks like a place or a man's name; it is a kind of tree.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an original version is the earliest one, the one later copies come after.

blocks.note: a machine that acts up malfunctions
a child who acts up carries on, misbehaves

annotation.surface: An ultimatum to a worker: down tools or keep going.
annotation.walkthrough: "Carry on" reads as continue; it is the British sense of making a fuss.
annotation.definitionFit: To act up is both to malfunction and to misbehave.

entries.clue: Some who believe toast is toast! (7)

indicatorNotes.toast!: If something is toast it is finished, wrecked, so TOAST IS is wrecked into new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: A remark that some people treat toast as an article of faith.
annotation.walkthrough: The same word does two jobs: the first "toast" is fodder, the second is slang for ruined and is the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Taoists follow Taoism, the Chinese religion and philosophy of the Tao, the Way.

blocks.note: got = became, as in got angry
h = hot, as on a tap
sandpaper is rough

annotation.surface: A man's face going red and stubbly, like after a hot shave gone wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: "Face" looks like the noun that became hot; it is a verb, as in to face an ordeal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to face an ordeal is to experience and endure it.

entries.clue: Not like one in Paris Match (7)

blocks.note: un = one in French
to match is to equal

annotation.surface: A caption about the French magazine Paris Match.
annotation.walkthrough: Paris Match is a real French magazine, which hides the split between "Paris" and "Match".
annotation.definitionFit: Things that are unequal are not like each other.

entries.clue: Goes on about turning point for mothers (14)

indicatorNotes.about: About means around, so PROGRESSES goes round the reversed point.
indicatorNotes.turning: Turning means reversing, so TINE is read backwards as ENIT.

blocks.note: to progress is to go on; ENIT goes in after PROG
a tine is a point, a prong of a fork or antler

annotation.surface: Someone droning on about the menopause, the turning point for mothers.
annotation.walkthrough: "Turning point" reads as one phrase; split it into the reversal indicator and the word to reverse.
annotation.definitionFit: A progenitress is a female ancestor, one who gives rise to offspring.

indicatorNotes.coming back: What comes back returns the way it came, so TRAMS reads backwards.

blocks.note: streetcar is the American word for a tram; the plural is read backwards

annotation.surface: Trams returning to city streets as something fashionable again.
annotation.walkthrough: "Coming back into fashion" reads as one phrase; the break falls after "back".
annotation.definitionFit: Someone smart dresses fashionably; the question mark admits the definition is stretched.

indicatorNotes.unopened: An unopened bottle keeps its first part out of reach; here the word loses its first letter.

blocks.note: TOKAY, a Hungarian dessert wine, without its first letter

annotation.surface: A sommelier's verdict on a good wine still in its unopened bottle.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fine wine" reads as a single phrase; "Fine" is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean acceptable, all right.

blocks.note: OB = old boy, a former pupil; old boys come together at a reunion
a scene is a locale, where something happens

annotation.surface: A dirty venue picked for a school reunion.
annotation.walkthrough: The old boys' scene is the setting where old boys gather, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: Obscene means filthy, offensive to decency.

blocks.note: to do a bed is to make it
a = one
a bunk is a bed

annotation.surface: A magician's request: make one bed vanish.
annotation.walkthrough: To do a bunk is British slang for running off without warning, often to dodge a bill.
annotation.definitionFit: Doing a bunk means disappearing suddenly, usually to escape something.

entries.clue: Some casinos identify end of game (2-4)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some means part of, so the answer is part of the words that follow.

blocks.note: casiNOS IDEntify

annotation.surface: Casinos that can tell when a game is over.
annotation.walkthrough: No-side is the old rugby term for the final whistle.
annotation.definitionFit: A rugby term: once the final whistle blows the players are no longer on opposing sides, so the phrase marks the finish.

blocks.note: guys = men
a tally is a running score

annotation.surface: Men keeping count in their heads during a game.
annotation.walkthrough: "Keep" suggests one piece holding another, but here the guys simply have the score: MEN, then TALLY.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anything done in the head, without paper or speech, is done in mind.
